entities.label: Movement
entities.summary:
Neoplatonism, a profound strand of Platonic philosophy, systematically articulated by Plotinus in Rome around 245 CE, emerged as the dominant philosophical current of the late Roman Empire and exerted immense influence across the Byzantine East, the Islamic world, and medieval and Renaissance Europe. Rooted in the works of Plato, it reinterpreted his idealism through a complex metaphysical hierarchy, offering a sophisticated spiritual quest for union with the divine. Its significance lies in its role as a bridge between classical Greek thought and the burgeoning monotheistic traditions, shaping the intellectual landscape for over a millennium.

The core of Neoplatonic thought posits an emanating cosmos originating from an utterly transcendent, ineffable 'One' or 'Good,' which gives rise to intellect (Nous), soul (Psyche), and finally the material world. Key figures like Plotinus, whose teachings were compiled by Porphyry into the *Enneads*, and later Iamblichus and Proclus, elaborated on this system, incorporating elements of Pythagoreanism, Aristotelianism, and Stoicism, alongside ritualistic and theurgic practices in later stages. Major centers of Neoplatonic study flourished in Alexandria, Rome, and Athens, with the Athenian Academy, re-founded by Plutarch of Athens, serving as a bastion of pagan philosophy until its closure by Emperor Justinian I in 529 CE.
